finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar makes a server-side axios.get to an attacker-supplied URL. The only check is a string prefix match on https://, so private/internal hosts pass, and axios follows redirects (default maxRedirects, version not confirmed since there is no package.json) to http:// targets, bypassing the https check.
finding.source: req.body.avatarUrl (server.js:10), from the JSON body of POST /profile/avatar

trace.note: typeof string check and url.startsWith("https://") only; no host, IP-range, port or redirect validation
url passed directly to axios.get, redirects followed by default
only img.data.length is returned, so exploitation is blind (reachability, port and size oracles, GET side effects)

finding.guards_checked: Type check (string) passes attacker strings. Scheme check is a prefix match, not URL parsing, so it does not constrain host. No hostname allowlist, no DNS/IP check for loopback, RFC1918 or link-local (169.254.169.254), no maxRedirects:0, no beforeRedirect or lookup hook, no timeout or maxContentLength.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js:11 is a typeof check plus `url.startsWith("https://")`, a prefix match that does not constrain the host. No hostname allowlist, IP/private-range check, maxRedirects:0, or timeout exists anywhere in server.js.
verdict.reason: The attacker-controlled `req.body.avatarUrl` (server.js:10) from the unauthenticated POST /profile/avatar route (server.js:9) reaches `axios.get` at server.js:14 with only a scheme-prefix check at server.js:11, so an attacker can point the server at internal hosts such as http://users.internal:8080 or 169.254.169.254 (the response size is returned at server.js:15, which is a blind oracle). The redirect-to-http bypass claim is plausible but not needed for the finding, and the axios version is unconfirmed because there is no package.json.

finding.claim: Not reported. GET /users/:id requests a fixed host (USER_SVC, server.js:7). The id is encodeURIComponent'd (server.js:19), so the attacker cannot change host, scheme or port, and cannot inject / ? #. Only a dot-segment (id=..) can alter the path on the same internal host.

trace.note: id interpolated into path on fixed host

finding.guards_checked: Fixed host constant, encodeURIComponent, Express segment matching (no / inside :id). Residual same-host dot-segment path manipulation only.

verdict.guard_found: encodeURIComponent at server.js:19 encodes "/", "?", "#" and other reserved characters, so the id cannot change host, scheme, port, or add a query or fragment. The fixed base URL at server.js:7 pins the host. The only remaining manipulation is a whole-segment ".." or "." (not encoded by encodeURIComponent), which moves the path up at most to /v1/ on the same internal host.
verdict.reason: The candidate's trace is accurate (server.js:7, 19, 20), and the attacker-controlled id at server.js:18-19 cannot change host, scheme, or port because of the fixed USER_SVC constant at server.js:7 and encodeURIComponent at server.js:19, so no SSRF is reportable at line 20; the only residual is a dot-segment path move to /v1/ on the same host. Separately, the avatar endpoint at server.js:11-14 is not covered by this verdict: its `startsWith("https://")` check at line 11 is a prefix check that does not close SSRF, so a full attacker-chosen https URL reaches axios.get at line 14 and should be reviewed as its own finding.
